title: Understanding Bulgaria's April 2026 election
lede: Who won, how Bulgaria turns votes into seats, and what a stable majority after years of snap elections means for Sofia and for Europe. Based on the Central Election Commission's final results, as of 10 November 2026.

stats.l: seats won by Progressive Bulgaria (121 is a majority)

visual_note: Five forces cleared the 4% threshold. BSP – United Left, which sat in the outgoing governing coalition, fell out of Parliament. Seats are final CEC figures; turnout was about 51%.

cells: Former president Rumen Radev's new movement; centre-left, socially conservative
Centre-right, led by ex-PM Boyko Borisov
Movement for Rights and Freedoms; strong with Bulgaria's Turkish minority

table.note: Vote shares are of valid votes. Another 50,733 voters chose “I do not support anyone”.

elects: All 240 members of the National Assembly, Bulgaria's one-chamber parliament, for up to four years. The election was called early after the previous government, led by GERB with the Socialists, resigned in December 2025 following weeks of street protests over the 2026 budget and corruption.

Voters choose a party list, not a person. The Assembly then elects the prime minister. Former president Rumen Radev left the presidency to lead the list of Progressive Bulgaria, a three-party alliance.

system.oneline: Proportional representation with a 4% bar: a party's share of the vote becomes a near-equal share of seats, but only for parties above the line.

steps.p: Voters pick one party or coalition in their region. They can add a preference for one candidate on that list. The country is split into 31 multi-member districts; the map here shows the 28 provinces, with Sofia shown as one.
Votes for parties below the nationwide threshold are dropped, so the remaining parties' shares are scaled up. That is how a 44.6% share turned into 131 of 240 seats, 54.6%.

steps.h: Seats are shared out by quota
steps.p: Seats are allocated in proportion to votes using a quota-and-remainder method, then filled from each party's regional lists. Bulgarians abroad vote too.

The president hands the largest parliamentary group a mandate to form a government. Parliament elects it by a simple majority. Here one group holds that majority alone, which had not happened in recent Bulgarian history.

home: The headline is stability. Seven elections in the previous five years had produced fragile coalitions and caretaker governments. A single group with 131 seats can pass a budget and legislation without bargaining, and Radev's government survived a confidence vote on 8 May.

home.p: Bulgaria joined the euro in January 2026, and prices became the main grievance. The fall of the last government came after protests over a budget with higher taxes and social contributions. Radev criticised euro adoption but analysts do not expect him to reverse it.
Voters rewarded Radev for change, but he has been vague on policy. Corruption and judicial reform, long conditions for EU funds, are where the new majority will be tested first.

world.p: Radev condemned Russia's 2022 invasion but opposes military aid to Ukraine, has criticised EU sanctions, and objected to a 10-year defence pact Bulgaria signed with Kyiv in March. He has called for “practical relations with Russia”. Expect Sofia to stop short of vetoes but to sound more sceptical in EU talks.

The European Council on Foreign Relations expects rhetoric closer to Hungary's Viktor Orbán but behaviour closer to Slovakia's Robert Fico. Bulgaria depends heavily on EU funds and is a NATO member, which limits how far it can drift. The new foreign minister has stressed a Euro-Atlantic orientation.
EU decisions on sanctions, Ukraine financing and energy need unanimity or large majorities. One more hesitant government on the Black Sea flank adds friction, even without a veto.

otherway.h: A fragmented result, the ninth election in view
p: Polls before the vote pointed to five or six forces and no clear winner. Without a majority, Bulgaria would probably have faced another round of coalition haggling among GERB, PP–DB and others, and a real chance of a ninth election.

That coalition would most likely have kept the traditional pro-EU line on Ukraine and sanctions, but it would have been weaker at home. The trade the voters made was stability and a more sceptical tone abroad in place of a steadier foreign-policy line and a weaker government.
